content.text:
**Cause:** in `generated/registry.py`, `ACCOUNTS` is a Python **set**, not a list. Python changes the iteration order of a set of strings every time it starts, unless `PYTHONHASHSEED` is fixed (hash randomisation). Each of the five functions starts from set order, then sorts on a value that can tie between accounts, and never breaks the tie by name. Python's sort keeps tied items in the order they arrived, so the result changes from run to run. That's why a rerun of the same commit can pass.

All five functions have docstrings promising that ties go to the name that sorts first. None of them does that.

| Test | Code | What ties |
|---|---|---|
| `test_display_order` | `ledger/sync.py:30` sorts by balance only | accounts with equal balance (`travel`/`business` swapped in run 1) |
| `test_header_same_day_by_name` | `ledger/statement.py:24-25` sorts by last date only | accounts last active on the same day |
| `test_worst_offender_tie_named_by_name` | `ledger/limits.py:43` uses `max()` with no tie-break | accounts equally far over their limit; `max()` returns whichever comes first in set order |
| `test_same_headroom_by_name` | `ledger/rebalance.py:14-15` sorts by headroom only | accounts with the same headroom |
| `test_matches_golden` | `ledger/export.py:47` sorts by row count only | accounts with the same row count in a month, so the output differs from the golden file |

**Reproduced locally:** I ran those five test modules four times with no code changes. Each run failed a different set of tests: four failures, four, one, three. Together the runs hit all five tests, which matches the CI pattern. My attempt to pin specific hash seeds was blocked by the sandbox, so the link to the hash seed is inferred, not shown seed by seed. But a set of strings is the only thing in this code whose order changes between processes; the code has no randomness or time dependence.

**Decision for you before any fix:** the set order comes from `generated/`, which can't be edited by hand. So the fix has to go in `ledger/`. The usual approach is to add the name as a second sort key in each of the five places, for example `key=lambda a: (-totals[a], a)`. That makes the code do what its docstrings promise, whatever order the set comes in.

Another option is to ask the schema team to generate `ACCOUNTS` as a list. That alone wouldn't satisfy the docstrings, though: ties would follow the schema's order, not name order.

**Separate problem:** CI has no `PYTHONHASHSEED` set, so these failures look random. Fixing the tie-breaks removes the dependency on it either way.
